title: Electronic Structure and Superconductivity in La$_{1.55}$Sr$_{0.45}$CuO$_4$/La$_2$CuO$_4$ Artificial High-$T_c$ Superlattices Probed by Hard and Soft X-ray Spectroscopy
authors: U. M. Jayathilake, S. Sheikh, T. -L. Lee, C. Klewe, G. Logvenov, G. Campi, A. Bianconi, A. X. Gray
abstract: In La$_{1.55}$Sr$_{0.45}$CuO$_4$/La$_2$CuO$_4$ (LSCO/LCO) artificial high-$T_c$ superlattices (AHTS), grown by quantum material design, the superconducting dome can be tuned by varying the geometric ratio $L/d$, where $L$ is the LCO layer thickness and $d$ is the superlattice nanoscale period. Here, we combine hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES) and polarization-dependent soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) to probe how the electronic structure evolves across the $L/d$-tuned superconducting dome. We observe systematic chemical-potential evolution across the series, together with enhanced spectral weight near the Fermi level, enhanced local and non-local screening signatures, and increased in-plane orbital polarization near the top of the dome. Together, these spectroscopic signatures provide insight into the emergence of Fano-Feshbach resonant superconductivity in the LSCO/LCO AHTS series.
summary: This work uses hard and soft X-ray spectroscopy to map the electronic structure of artificial high-Tc superlattices ($	ext{LSCO}/	ext{LCO}$) as the superconducting dome is tuned by changing the layer thickness ratio ($L/d$). The results demonstrate that the optimal superconducting state correlates with spectroscopic signatures indicating the system is tuned near a Van Hove Singularity, providing strong experimental evidence for the electronic mechanism driving high-Tc superconductivity in these engineered structures.
main_problem: To determine how the electronic structure evolves across the superconducting dome in artificial high-Tc superlattices (AHTS) as a function of geometric tuning.
main_result: Spectroscopic signatures (DOS enhancement, screening, orbital polarization) are strongest near $L/d = 0.67$, supporting a model where superconductivity emerges from tuning the system toward a Van Hove Singularity (VHS) via an electronic topological transition.
method: The study combines Hard X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (HAXPES) and polarization-dependent Soft X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) to probe both occupied and unoccupied electronic states.
model_or_system: The system is the $	ext{La}_{1.55}	ext{Sr}_{0.45}	ext{CuO}_4/	ext{La}_2	ext{CuO}_4$ superlattice, whose superconducting dome is tuned by varying the geometric ratio $L/d$. The analysis is guided by the Bianconi-Perali-Valletta (BPV) framework, which predicts superconductivity enhancement near a Lifshitz electronic transition.
key_observables: Leading-edge spectral weight ($\Delta S$), chemical potential ($\mu$) shifts (from $	ext{La } 3d$), local/non-local screening signatures ($	ext{Cu } 2p$), and in-plane orbital polarization ($	ext{Cu } L_{2,3}	ext{-edge}$ XLD).
important_parameters: The geometric ratio $L/d$ (e.g., 0.44, 0.67, 0.78, 0.89) acts as the primary tuning parameter, controlling the effective hole doping and proximity to the predicted optimal doping regime.
main_assumptions: The superconducting dome behavior is governed by the BPV framework, linking superconductivity to the proximity of the chemical potential to a Van Hove Singularity (VHS) induced by the superlattice periodicity.
figures_summary: The figures likely show systematic trends in core-level shifts, spectral weight enhancements near the Fermi level, and polarization-dependent spectral features that correlate with the measured $T_c$ dome.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents evidence from multiple spectroscopic techniques (HAXPES, XAS) across the series of superlattices, correlating the observed electronic structure changes (e.g., $\mu$ evolution, DOS changes) with the known superconducting dome structure.
why_interesting: The use of advanced X-ray spectroscopy to map out the electronic structure evolution across a quantum-engineered superconducting phase is highly relevant for understanding unconventional superconductivity mechanisms in correlated materials.
